beginner.label: Beginner
beginner.desc: No theory background assumed: start with the feel, then see how it's used. Every term gets translated into plain language the first time it appears.

learner.label: Some Theory
learner.tagline: Turn functional harmony into a map
learner.desc: Keeps standard terms and degree logic, and adds concrete progressions, resolution directions, and paths you can actually practice.

pro.label: Musician
pro.desc: Focuses on guide tones, tension tones, voicings, substitution, and modal interchange, directly serving writing, arranging, and recording.

levelHint.beginner: Zero-background view: hear the feel first, then learn how to use it
levelHint.learner: Some-theory view: keeps degree, function, and resolution terminology
levelHint.pro: Musician view: guide tones, tension structure, and arranging detail

levelBanner.beginner: Reading in Beginner view · every explanation starts in plain language
levelBanner.learner: Reading in Some Theory view · degree and function terms are in place
levelBanner.pro: Reading in Musician view · straight to substitution, tension, and voice-leading engineering

focusLead.beginner: What it sounds like, when to use it, and where your hands go, all laid out below.
focusLead.learner: An integrated view of function, construction, voice leading, and assigned scale.
focusLead.pro: An engineering view of guide tones, tension structure, and substitute voicings.

gridHint.beginner: No need to memorize names: pick by feel first, whether stable, suspenseful, tense, or open.
gridHint.learner: Filter by category, or search chord symbols, qualities, and use cases.
gridHint.pro: Locate chord material fast by tension level and instrument suitability.

searchHint.beginner: Just type a name you know, such as maj7, sus4, or ninth chord.
searchHint.learner: Supports symbols, qualities, functions, and context keywords.
searchHint.pro: Supports term searches such as alt, upper structure, slash, and tension.

scaleLead.beginner: This group of notes is your safe zone: start by playing inside these notes.
scaleLead.learner: The natural scale of the current mode and the function of each degree.
scaleLead.pro: A comparison of modal scales, degree functions, and available tension tones.

knowledgeLead.beginner: Four of the most practical directions: grab one and start practicing.
knowledgeLead.learner: Build a framework from four dimensions: classical, jazz, modal, and arranging.
knowledgeLead.pro: Puts style grammar, modal systems, and arranging habits on the same map.

historyLead.beginner: No need to memorize dates: just see how harmony evolved step by step into what it is today.
historyLead.learner: From ancient Greece to jazz and pop, understand how functional harmony evolved.
historyLead.pro: The evolution of tuning systems, notation, and harmonic grammar, and its impact on contemporary arranging.

lead.beginner: The distance between two notes decides whether they sound close together or wide apart.
lead.learner: Degree, semitone count, and consonance are the foundation of ear training and harmonic writing.
lead.pro: Interval tendencies, resolution paths, and function within a voicing.

referenceLead.beginner: Treat this table as a distance chart: memorize the two ends first, the most stable and the most tense.
referenceLead.learner: A quick reference to how the 13 basic intervals sound and how they are commonly used.
referenceLead.pro: A complete reference of interval, tension, and resolution direction.

lead.beginner: Check whether this progression feels like setting out, leaving, and coming home.
lead.learner: Evaluate direction and cadence along the T–S–D–T function chain.
lead.pro: Four-dimension scoring: voice leading, functional strength, tension release, and stylistic fit.

emptyLane.beginner: Tap chords on the left and line them up into a harmonic route.
emptyLane.learner: Add degrees from the chord material to build an analyzable functional progression.
emptyLane.pro: Drag in degree material and see the function chain, voice smoothness, and substitution suggestions in real time.

galleryLead.beginner: Each mode is a kind of weather. Hear the brightness or darkness first, then remember one note that stands out.
galleryLead.learner: Grouped by church modes, melodic minor, pentatonic, and symmetrical scales, compare the characteristic notes.
galleryLead.pro: Search by mode family, focusing on characteristic tones, avoid notes, and chord–scale mapping.

detailLead.beginner: Hear how bright or dark it is first, then see which chords it fits.
detailLead.learner: A full view of characteristic tones, common progressions, and improv landing points.
detailLead.pro: A comparison of characteristic tones, avoid notes, upper structures, and substitute scales.

lead.beginner: Four voices are like four tracks: the goal is fewer leaps, fewer collisions, and each one moving smoothly.
lead.learner: Watch how guide tones, common tones, and parallel fifths and octaves are handled.
lead.pro: SATB voice engineering: spacing, guide-tone resolution, and hidden and parallel rules.

termsLead.beginner: When a foreign term stumps you, start with the plain-language one-liner.
termsLead.learner: A master table of terms in five languages, playing techniques, and arranging practice.
termsLead.pro: A five-language workflow reference for arranging, articulation, tempo, and form terms.

atlasLead.beginner: Learn the shape of one position first, then connect them slowly.
atlasLead.learner: A systematic atlas of CAGED, 3NP, pentatonic blues, and modern pop fingerings.
atlasLead.pro: Triple labeling of position systems, interval degrees, and actual note names.

lead.beginner: Imitate one phrase, change two notes, and eventually make it your own.
lead.learner: Filter by style, difficulty, and technique, and analyze where each phrase lands.
lead.pro: A reusable library of vocabulary, rhythmic grammar, and harmonic landing points.

lead.beginner: Wrong answers are fine: remember the sound and the shape first.
lead.learner: Drill by level and question type, and use the mistake log to find weak spots.
lead.pro: Leveled question bank and mistake review for targeted work on harmony, intervals, and terminology.

correct.beginner: Correct! Remember this feeling so it comes automatically next time.
correct.learner: Right reasoning path: identify the quality first, then rule out the distractors.
correct.pro: Correct. Worth also double-checking enharmonics, inversions, and alternate readings.

wrong.beginner: It's okay: note the correct answer first, then look back at the question.
wrong.learner: The mistake usually comes from one key condition: go back to the definition and check each item.
wrong.pro: Review: confirm whether the slip was chord quality, enharmonics, or a rule detail.

autoNext.beginner: Moving on to the next question shortly.
autoNext.learner: Moving on shortly, or tap Next question.
autoNext.pro: Auto-advances shortly, or move on manually.

lead.beginner: Fill in the skeleton first, which note on each beat, then add technique.
lead.learner: Enter by beat position and duration, and check the voices against the staff.
lead.pro: Cross-check tab against staff notation, and check technique and voice rules before exporting.

noMatch.beginner: Nothing in this part of the sky: try a simpler word.
noMatch.learner: No matches: adjust your keywords or category filters.
noMatch.pro: No matching entries: check spelling and synonyms, or clear the filters.

noData.beginner: This is still empty: add something to get started.
noData.learner: No data yet; it will show up here once you add it.
noData.pro: Empty state: no data has been created yet.

voice.beginner: How to stack the notes so it sounds good

style.beginner: Which kind of song it fits
